scope: One additional reef fish for the guide, illustrative encounters and optional identification. Show an unsexed cream-and-pink mottled example with fixed contact points and gentle upper-body sway.
iucnYearConvention: LC assessed 5 March 2015; published 2016. The indexed primary IUCN DOI page supplied the complete assessment metadata; direct DOI and species-page fetches returned 403. Do not mistake publication year for assessment year.

specimens.name: Leaf scorpionfish
marks: A deep body is flattened strongly from side to side
A tall sail-like back fin runs almost continuously into the rounded tail
Small skin fringes surround the mouth and rise above the eyes
Broad fan-shaped side fins support a mottled, rough-skinned body
specimens.role: A small bottom-dwelling ambush predator of fishes and crustaceans.
specimens.fact: It periodically sheds its outer skin, removing attached growth. Its colour can change after a moult.
specimens.habitat: Tropical Indo-Pacific reef bottoms, including sand, rock, coral and algae-covered areas.
specimens.diet: Small fishes and crustaceans caught by ambush.
specimens.behavior: Often stays in place and rocks with water movement, resembling a loose leaf. The gentle sway here illustrates that camouflage.
specimens.observe: Look for the flattened outline, tall continuous back fin and small facial fringes. Compare the red lionfish’s separate long spines and striped body. Colour varies widely, so use shape as well as colour. Observe without touching its venomous spines.

claimSupport.acceptedName: CSIRO CAAB identifies Taenianotus triacanthus as accepted; the current indexed Eschmeyer catalog agrees. The species account and primary assessment use the same name.
claimSupport.shape: Smithsonian documents a deep, highly compressed body, oblique mouth, high sail-like dorsal with XII spines, last soft ray attached to the upper caudal, large fan-like pectorals and rounded caudal. Museums Victoria corroborates skin papillae and mouth appendages; the Australian Museum field guide adds above-eye appendages. This illustrative mesh is not a complete diagnostic key.
claimSupport.habitatDiet: Smithsonian supplies demersal sand, rock, coral and algal habitats and fishes/crustaceans as food. Museums Victoria independently identifies an ambush predator; no aquarium-care claims are imported.
claimSupport.motionColour: Museums Victoria describes current-associated rocking, varied whitish/pink/yellow/brown/greenish appearances and skin shedding to remove growth. The cream/pink model is one illustrative unsexed variant; no sex, age, fixed moulting interval or universally pink appearance is inferred.
claimSupport.sizeDepth: Museums Victoria gives a maximum 10 cm total length and 1–135 m. Smithsonian gives 10 cm and 5–135 m. The museum interval is selected as encounter metadata, not a hard biological limit or equal habitat suitability. Nominal .10 m represents an illustrative individual near the reported maximum, not a typical measured adult.
claimSupport.conservation: Indexed primary IUCN DOI account names Motomura and Matsuura (2016), status LC, assessment date 2015-03-05, with unknown trend. FishBase independently reports LC and the same assessment date. Smithsonian’s unupdated Not evaluated / Listed field is not adopted.
claimSupport.comparison: The one-way red-lionfish link contrasts two scorpionfish silhouettes already represented in the guide; it does not claim they are the closest species-level lookalikes. The existing lionfish entry is preserved.

specimens.caution: No special fluorescence, human-like emotions, rapid swimming, obligate lifelong site fidelity, fixed moulting schedule, sex or maturity label. Spines are venomous, but this guide supplies no handling or medical instructions.
